title: Senior At-Home Care
desc: Plan and deliver safe, respectful at-home support for older adults: daily living, safety, medicines reminders, dignity and when to call for help.
outcomes: Explain the needs, rights and dignity of an older person at home.
Find fall, fire and medicine risks in a home.
Judge when a situation needs a professional or emergency help.
Build a written care routine and a family communication plan.
task: Produce a person-centred home care plan for a practice case, with a home safety check, daily routine, emergency card and carer wellbeing plan.
condition: A practice case or a consenting family, a phone, forms, two peers and a qualified nurse or care mentor. Nursing procedures are outside scope.
standard: Plan respects the person's wishes; safety check finds and fixes at least 8 risks; emergency card is complete; no clinical task is done outside training; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Family carers, home-care assistants, community volunteers, care entrepreneurs.
evidence: care plan, home safety checklist, routine, emergency card, carer plan
modules: Respect and dignity first
Understand
Good care starts with the person, not the task. Older adults have a lifetime of skills, habits and wishes that should shape their care.
Ask what they want, offer real choices and use their preferred name.
Protect privacy in washing, dressing and toilet care; knock, close doors, cover with towels.
Never talk about the person as if they are not present and never treat an adult like a child.
Involve them in decisions, including small ones like clothes and meals.
Mr Rao likes tea at 7 am and a walk at 5 pm. The carer plans the day around these, keeps the bathroom door closed during care and asks before each step.
Write a "what matters to me" page with a real or practice person using their own words.
Page lists at least eight preferences in the person's words and is signed off by them.
Home safety check
Analyse
Most harm to older people at home is preventable. A structured check finds risks before an accident.
Falls: loose rugs, poor light, wet floors, no grab rails, clutter on stairs.
Fire and electrical hazards: frayed cables, overloaded sockets, unattended cooking, gas leaks.
Medicine storage and bathroom hot water.
Easy-to-reach items, a clear path to the toilet and night lights.
A carer removes a loose mat, fits a night light and rail by the bed and moves the kettle to counter height. Night-time stumbles stop within a month.
Complete a home safety checklist for one home and photograph before and after each fix.
At least eight risks found, each with a fix, an owner and a date.
Daily living support
Apply
Support independence rather than replacing it.
Meals and drinks: offer fluids through the day and watch weight and appetite.
Mobility: assist with walking aids, use correct lifting aids and ask for training before lifting.
Hygiene and dressing: do with, not for, whenever possible.
Rest, activity and company all matter.
The carer lays out clothes in order and lets Mrs Iyer dress herself, stepping in only for buttons. Her confidence and her strength improve over weeks.
Plan a full day routine with times for meals, fluids, movement, rest and social contact.
Routine covers all five areas and respects the person's preferences.
Medicines and health reminders
Apply
Carers remind and observe; clinicians decide.
Use a pill organiser prepared by a pharmacist or nurse.
Record each dose taken or refused; never change doses or share medicines.
Report new symptoms, falls and side effects promptly.
Keep a list of medicines and allergies.
A weekly box with morning and evening slots reduces missed doses from five a week to one. The carer records each tick and reports a dizzy spell to the nurse.
Create a reminder chart and a record sheet from a sample prescription list.
Chart matches the list exactly and a nurse mentor confirms it.
Mind, mood and memory
Apply
Loneliness, low mood and forgetfulness are common but not inevitable.
Keep a regular routine, calendars and clocks; label doors.
Encourage activity, light and conversation; arrange visits and calls.
Be patient with repeated questions; redirect kindly rather than arguing.
Sudden confusion can signal infection or illness; seek medical help promptly.
A daily 15-minute walk and a call to a grandchild improves sleep and mood. A sudden change in behaviour triggers a call to the doctor, who finds a urine infection.
Plan a weekly social and activity schedule with five activities.
Schedule includes social, physical and mental activities and respects interests.
Emergencies and when to call
Evaluate
Know the line between watching and acting.
Call emergency services for chest pain, stroke signs, serious fall, breathing trouble, heavy bleeding.
Call the doctor for fever, new pain, poor eating or drinking, or sudden change.
Keep an emergency card by the door and in the phone.
Stay calm, note times and what happened.
Face drooping and slurred speech appear at 10:15. The carer calls emergency services, notes the time and stays with the person.
Make an emergency card with numbers, allergies, medicines, conditions and contacts.
Card is complete and tested by a family member.
Family and carer wellbeing
Evaluate
Carers burn out when they carry everything alone.
Share tasks and take planned breaks.
Use a shared log or group message.
Seek local support groups and respite care.
Watch your own sleep, mood and health.
Three siblings take alternate weekends; the main carer takes one free day each week, and her stress score falls.
Write a carer wellbeing plan naming who does what and when.
Plan has names, days and a review date.
Review and improve
Create
Care plans change as needs change.
Review monthly or after any event such as a fall or hospital stay.
Track weight, sleep, mood and falls.
Celebrate good days and note what worked.
Update the plan with the person and family.
After a fall, a rail is added, a physiotherapist visits and the walking aid is changed. No further falls occur in three months.
Present your care plan and review.
Changes are dated and agreed with the person.
quiz: Why use their words?
It keeps dignity and choice. (Covered in module 1: Respect and dignity first. To pass that module: Page lists at least eight preferences in the person's words and is signed off by them.)
Name three fall risks.
Loose rugs, poor light, wet floors. (Covered in module 2: Home safety check. To pass that module: At least eight risks found, each with a fix, an owner and a date.)
Who decides doses?
The prescriber. (Covered in module 3: Daily living support. To pass that module: Routine covers all five areas and respects the person's preferences.)
When call emergency?
Chest pain, stroke signs, serious fall, breathing trouble. (Covered in module 4: Medicines and health reminders. To pass that module: Chart matches the list exactly and a nurse mentor confirms it.)
What is "do with, not for"?
Support independence by helping only as needed. (Covered in module 5: Mind, mood and memory. To pass that module: Schedule includes social, physical and mental activities and respects interests.)
Name one mood tip.
Daily activity and social contact. (Covered in module 6: Emergencies and when to call. To pass that module: Card is complete and tested by a family member.)
What is sudden confusion a sign of?
Possible illness; seek help. (Covered in module 7: Family and carer wellbeing. To pass that module: Plan has names, days and a review date.)
What goes on an emergency card?
Numbers, allergies, medicines, contacts. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: Changes are dated and agreed with the person.)
Why carer breaks?
To avoid burnout. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: Changes are dated and agreed with the person.)
How often review?
Monthly or after any event. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: Changes are dated and agreed with the person.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
local: Care rules, licences and background checks differ by place.
